text: Real files have rows that don't parse cleanly, and real business rules get violated — a negative quantity that's perfectly valid as a number but wrong as an order. This lesson is about handling both kinds of failure without your script crashing.

Catching ValueError specifically, instead of a bare except, is the whole point here. int of an empty string or float of N slash A raises exactly that ValueError in a real export with a blank or corrupted numeric field — and because you caught that specific type, a genuinely different bug, like a typo'd column name raising KeyError, still surfaces loudly instead of getting silently swallowed by the same except block.

Order 1014 has a quantity of negative one, and int of negative one doesn't raise anything — Python parses it just fine, because it's numerically valid. It's only wrong as a business rule. So you raise the exception yourself inside a helper function, which plugs your own validation straight into Python's normal error handling instead of scattering if-slash-continue checks through the loop.

else runs only if the try block did not raise — it's the "it succeeded" branch, kept separate so you can tell at a glance which lines are the risky operation. finally runs no matter what, exception or not, which is exactly why cleanup code like closing a connection belongs there.

Five pieces, five jobs. try and except run the risky code and catch a specific failure. raise lets you trigger your own exception from validation logic. else fires only on success. And finally fires either way, success or failure, for cleanup that absolutely has to happen.
With error handling in place, next lesson moves outside your own files entirely: calling a real, live REST API with the requests library, against GitHub's actual public API.
